contributions.headingText: Fibromatosis is a locally aggressive but non-metastasizing fibroblastic and myofibroblastic neoplasm with an infiltrative growth pattern and propensity for local recurrence.

Superficial fibromatoses, such as palmar and plantar fibromatoses, occur in the hands and feet {34225446}. Deep desmoid-type fibromatoses commonly arise in the deep soft tissues of the extremities, abdominal and chest walls, breast, retroperitoneum, and abdominal cavity, and less commonly in the head and neck and paraspinal regions {20830713; 21844500; 23532110}. The FNAB findings in these lesions are the same, and therefore they are presented together in this section.

Palmar fibromatosis, also known as Dupuytren contracture, tends to grow slowly and to manifest as one or more nodules of firm tissue leading to induration and in some instances contracture of the volar aspect of the hand and fingers. Plantar fibromatosis causes deformation of the plantar aspect of the feet; the changes are relatively less severe than those associated with palmar fibromatosis, but they can cause significant pain. Abdominal wall lesions referred to as desmoid tumours are typically centred on the rectus musculature and often develop in peripartum women. Intra-abdominal forms of fibromatosis occur within the pelvis, in the mesentery, and very rarely in the pancreas {26215223; 34194727; 32857922}.

Both forms of fibromatosis occur in a wide age range, predominantly in young and middle-aged adults, although they can also occur in infants and children {16015632; 19950127; 22420727}. Women are twice as likely to be affected as men {7091046}. Paediatric patients presenting with a desmoid tumour should be evaluated for adenomatous polyposis coli, because this is often the first sign of an inherited syndrome involving mutation of the APC gene.

Desmoid fibromatoses may occur sporadically or in association with familial adenomatous polyposis, a variant of which is known as Gardner syndrome. An estimated 10–20% of desmoid tumours occur in association with familial adenomatous polyposis {16736290}. Patients with Gardner syndrome have germline mutations of the APC tumour suppressor gene, whereas patients with sporadic cases most often have point mutations of the gene that encodes for β-catenin (CTNNB1). Dysregulation of the β-catenin/WNT regulation pathway results in abnormal β-catenin accumulation in both the cytoplasm and nucleus of the tumours cells, as well as increased cellular proliferation {18722078; 17558858}.

The imaging features of fibromatosis, both the superficial and deep subtypes, are nonspecific. Lesions may appear circumscribed or ill defined. MRI signal intensity on T2-weighted imaging varies depending on the relative overall cellularity of the lesion {22109314; 16357411; 25782339}.

Fibromatosis is characterized by long, intersecting fascicles of cells that can span an entire low-power field of view. The tumour contains small to medium-sized vessels, occasionally in irregular or staghorn shapes. Other findings include occasional areas of oedema, areas of keloid-like collagen deposition, chronic inflammation, and focal nodular fasciitis–like regions. Individual tumour cells have thin and long eosinophilic cytoplasm but indistinct cytoplasmic borders. Nuclei tend to be fusiform or oval and fairly uniform in size and shape. Mitoses are very rare. As mentioned elsewhere, fibromatosis tends to infiltrate adjacent soft tissues. In skeletal muscle, fibromatosis often insinuates in and surrounds individual muscle bands.

Deep desmoid fibromatoses are commonly examined by FNAB, whereas plantar, palmar, and mesenteric fibromatoses rarely undergo FNAB. The differential diagnosis of fibromatosis includes a number of benign to low-grade lesions with a spindle cell pattern. Smears from desmoids may occasionally show a myxoid matrix, evoking the differential diagnosis of low-grade myxoid spindle cell lesions, such as nodular fasciitis or low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma (LGFMS). Nodular fasciitis can simulate fibromatosis in its clinical presentation involving skin and shows substantial overlap in cytomorphological features. It typically has a more dispersed population of cells and includes tissue fragments of these cells within a myxoid background, imparting a “tissue culture” appearance. Individual cells of nodular fasciitis show more variability and can display a range of sizes and shapes, with polygonal, epithelioid, or plasmacytoid cells. Fragments of collagenous and metachromatic stroma are frequently seen in smears from desmoids and are very rare in nodular fasciitis; ganglion-type cells and prominent nucleoli are a frequent and distinctive feature in samples of nodular fasciitis but are usually absent in fibromatoses {6942611; 27525591}.

Benign peripheral nerve sheath tumours, including schwannoma and neurofibroma, can also cause considerable diagnostic confusion. Both of these lesions are characterized by moderately cellular smears, often with fragments of metachromatic stromal material. Unlike in fibromatosis, however, the spindle cells of nerve sheath tumours have distinctive nuclear features of a marked curved or comma shape and tapered or pointed ends. In addition, many of the nuclei of nerve sheath tumours show distinctive intranuclear pseudoinclusions {16900474; 10319234}.

Myofibroblastoma also shows extensive overlap with fibromatosis, but it tends to be more superficially located and occurs preferentially in the breast, inguinal/pelvic regions, and gynaecological tract.

Another soft tissue lesion that can be difficult to distinguish from fibromatosis is low-grade myofibroblastic sarcoma, a rare neoplasm with wide anatomical site and age distributions and fibromatosis-like histopathological features {9777985; 15173943}. Smears of low-grade myofibroblastic sarcoma show spindle cells with elongated, fusiform, occasionally angulated nuclei with small nucleoli and more nuclear atypia than seen in desmoid tumours {30079453}.

One of the most difficult lesions to separate from fibromatosis is LGFMS. These two neoplasms share numerous features, including bland spindle cells, fragments of stroma and dispersed spindle cells or naked nuclei in the background, and finely granular nuclear chromatin that can show perinucleolar clearing (“vesicular” chromatin on Pap), although desmoid fibromatoses are less cellular {18637810}. ICC is very useful in this differential diagnosis.

Nuclear β-catenin staining is often used to confirm a fibromatosis and separate this entity from its look-alikes {15832090}, but this is not entirely specific: up to 20% of tumours either fail to stain or show a nonspecific cytoplasmic staining pattern {17711447}. Fibromatosis also expresses markers of myofibroblastic differentiation, including MSA and SMA. Desmin is usually negative but may show focal positivity. Helpful negative stains include EMA, CD34, S100, and KIT (CD117). S100 is strongly positive in nerve sheath tumours but negative in fibromatosis. Positive staining for CD34 is helpful in confirming a diagnosis of myofibroblastoma and excluding fibromatosis. Low-grade myofibroblastic sarcomas do not express nuclear β-catenin. LGFMS shows diffuse immunoreactivity for MUC4, a feature not identified in fibromatosis {21415703}, and LGFMS can also be confirmed by demonstrating the FUS::CREB3L2 or FUS::CREB3L1 fusion that characterizes this neoplasm.
